title: Ἕκτορος τάφος
about: Priam’s wagon reaches the gates, where the whole city has come out, and Andromache and Hecuba rush to take hold of Hector’s head; the old king has to ask the crowd to make way. In the house the dead man is laid on a corded bed, minstrels lead the dirges, and three women in turn lead off the lament. Andromache sees a widow’s life ahead and a child thrown from a tower, Hecuba marvels that he lies as fresh as one killed by Apollo’s gentle arrows, and Helen says that in twenty years Hector alone never spoke a harsh word to her. Priam tells the Trojans to bring wood and not to fear an ambush, for Achilles has promised no harm until the twelfth dawn. For nine days they bring wood; on the tenth they burn Hector, at dawn quench the pyre with wine, gather the white bones into a golden chest, bury it under a heaped mound with lookouts set round, and feast in Priam’s house.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδέ τις αὐτόθ’ ἐνὶ πτόλεϊ λίπετ’ ἀνὴρ
οὐδὲ γυνή·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and not any there in the city was left behind, man
nor woman;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and no one was left behind in the city, neither man nor woman;
sentences.n: Cassandra’s call (703–706) has worked: the whole city has come out. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ὣς ἔφατο with its last vowel dropped, ‘so she spoke’. πτόλεϊ is the dative of πτόλις, an older form of πόλις ‘city’, and λίπετ’ is λίπετο, the aorist middle of λείπω, ‘was left behind’. αὐτόθ’ is αὐτόθι ‘right there, on the spot’. The ano teleia leads into the reason, given in the next line.

sentences.t: πάντας γὰρ ἀάσχετον ἵκετο πένθος·
sentences.l: for upon all came unrestrainable grief;
sentences.i: for an unrestrainable grief came upon them all;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason: everyone had come out because grief reached them all. πάντας is the object of ἵκετο ‘came to, reached’, which takes the accusative of the people reached. ἀάσχετον ‘unrestrainable’ is ἀ- ‘not’ + a form of ἔχω ‘hold’: a grief not to be held back.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δὲ ξύμβληντο πυλάων νεκρὸν ἄγοντι.
sentences.l: And near the gates they met him, a corpse leading.
sentences.i: They met him near the gates as he brought the corpse.
sentences.n: The subject changes to the crowd, unnamed. ἀγχοῦ ‘near’ takes the genitive πυλάων ‘the gates’ (epic -άων for -ῶν). ξύμβληντο is the aorist middle of συμβάλλω, with the old spelling ξυν- for συν-: in the middle ‘meet’, with the dative. ἄγοντι ‘the one leading’ is Priam, bringing the corpse (νεκρόν) on the wagon.

sentences.t:
πρῶται τόν γ’ ἄλοχός τε φίλη καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
τιλλέσθην ἐπ’ ἄμαξαν ἐΰτροχον ἀΐξασαι
ἁπτόμεναι κεφαλῆς·
sentences.i: First of all his dear wife and his lady mother, darting up to the well-rolling wagon, tore their hair and laid hold of his head;
sentences.n: πρῶται ‘first’ agrees with the two women, and τόν γ’ ‘him’ is Hector. ἄλοχος ‘wife’ and μήτηρ ‘mother’ are Andromache and Hecuba, named at 723 and 747. τιλλέσθην is a dual (two women), the imperfect middle of τίλλω ‘pluck’; with no object the middle means ‘pluck oneself’, that is, tear one’s hair in grief. ἀΐξασαι ‘darting’ and ἁπτόμεναι ‘laying hold of’ are plural participles beside the dual verb; ἁπτόμεναι takes the genitive κεφαλῆς ‘head’. ἄμαξαν ἐΰτροχον ‘well-rolling wagon’ is a stock phrase, translated the same way each time.

sentences.t: κλαίων δ’ ἀμφίσταθ’ ὅμιλος.
sentences.l: and weeping stood around the throng.
sentences.i: and the throng stood weeping around them.
sentences.n: κλαίων is singular because it agrees with ὅμιλος ‘throng’, though the throng is many. ἀμφίσταθ’ is ἀμφίστατο, the imperfect of ἀμφίσταμαι ‘stand around’; its τ became θ before the rough breathing of ὅμιλος.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κε δὴ πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
Ἕκτορα δάκρυ χέοντες ὀδύροντο πρὸ πυλάων,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ἐκ δίφροιο γέρων λαοῖσι μετηύδα·
sentences.i: And they would have gone on lamenting Hector before the gates, shedding tears, all day long until the sun went down, if the old man had not spoken among the people from his chariot:
sentences.n: κε with the imperfect ὀδύροντο means ‘would have gone on lamenting’, and the condition εἰ μὴ … μετηύδα ‘if he had not spoken’ breaks it off. πρόπαν ἦμαρ is ‘all day long’; ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα ‘until the sun sinking’. δάκρυ χέοντες ‘a tear shedding’ is the stock phrase for weeping. ὀδύρομαι is ‘lament’. The old man is Priam, left unnamed; δίφρος is the chariot, and μετηύδα is the imperfect of μεταυδάω ‘speak among’. λαοῖσι is the epic dative plural.

sentences.t: εἴξατέ μοι οὐρεῦσι διελθέμεν·
sentences.l: “Give way to me, to the mules, to go through;
sentences.i: “Make way for me and the mules to go through;
sentences.n: Priam’s speech begins. εἴξατε is the aorist imperative of εἴκω ‘give way’ and takes the dative: μοι ‘to me’ and, beside it, οὐρεῦσι, the dative plural of οὐρεύς ‘mule’. διελθέμεν is the aorist infinitive of διέρχομαι ‘go through’, in the epic ending -έμεν (= διελθεῖν): ‘give way to me and the mules, to go through’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
ἄσεσθε κλαυθμοῖο, ἐπὴν ἀγάγωμι δόμον δέ.
sentences.l:
but afterwards
you shall take your fill of weeping, when I have led him home.”
sentences.i: after that you shall have your fill of weeping, once I have brought him home.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘but afterwards’ puts the crowd’s weeping after the homecoming. ἄσεσθε is from ἄω ‘satiate’; in the middle, with the genitive κλαυθμοῖο (epic -οιο = -οῦ), ‘take your fill of weeping’, read here with future sense. ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν ‘when’, and ἀγάγωμι the aorist subjunctive of ἄγω ‘lead’ with the old ending -μι; the object ‘him’ is understood. δόμον δέ is δόμονδε, ‘homeward’, with the suffix -δε of direction. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ διέστησαν καὶ εἶξαν ἀπήνῃ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they stood apart and gave way to the wagon.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they parted and made way for the wagon.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ὣς ἔφατο with its last vowel dropped and τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of the next word (οἳ), ‘so he spoke’. διέστησαν is the aorist of διίστημι, here intransitive: ‘stood apart’. εἶξαν is the aorist of εἴκω ‘give way’ (as in Priam’s εἴξατε), with the dative ἀπήνῃ ‘the wagon’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ εἰσάγαγον κλυτὰ δώματα, τὸν μὲν ἔπειτα
τρητοῖς ἐν λεχέεσσι θέσαν, παρὰ δ’ εἷσαν ἀοιδοὺς
θρήνων ἐξάρχους, οἵ τε στονόεσσαν ἀοιδὴν
οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐθρήνεον, ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γυναῖκες.
sentences.l:
And when they had led him into the famous halls, him then
on a bored bedstead they laid, and beside it seated minstrels,
leaders-off of dirges, who the groan-filled song
they on the one hand sang as a dirge, and in answer groaned the women.
sentences.i: When they had brought him into the famous halls, they laid him on a corded bedstead and seated minstrels beside it, leaders of the dirges, who sang the groan-filled song as a lament, while the women groaned in answer.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ εἰσάγαγον ‘and when they had led in’: εἰσάγαγον is the aorist of εἰσάγω without the augment. κλυτὰ δώματα is the stock ‘famous halls’. θέσαν = ἔθεσαν. τρητοῖς ἐν λεχέεσσι is ‘on a bored bedstead’, a frame with holes bored for the cords (λεχέεσσι is the poetic plural for one bed). ἀοιδοὺς θρήνων ἐξάρχους is ‘minstrels, leaders-off of dirges’: an ἔξαρχος is the one who starts the song and sets the others going, and a θρῆνος is a dirge. οἵ τε is the relative ‘who’ with the epic τε, and στονόεσσαν ‘groan-filled’ goes with ἀοιδήν ‘song’. οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐθρήνεον takes the minstrels up again after the relative, ‘they, on the one hand, sang the dirge’, and ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γυναῖκες is ‘and the women groaned in answer’.

sentences.t:
τῇσιν δ’ Ἀνδρομάχη λευκώλενος ἦρχε γόοιο
Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο κάρη μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσα·
sentences.l:
And for them Andromache, white-armed, began the lament,
the head of Hector, man-slaying, in her hands holding;
sentences.i: Among them white-armed Andromache began the lament, holding in her hands the head of man-slaying Hector;
sentences.n: τῇσιν ‘for them’ is the women. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ and ἀνδροφόνοιο ‘man-slaying’ are stock epithets, translated the same way each time. ἦρχε γόοιο is ‘began the lament’, ἄρχω with the genitive; Hecuba and Helen will ‘lead off’ (ἐξῆρχε) theirs after her. A γόος is a personal lament sung over the dead. κάρη is the accusative of κάρη ‘head’, and μετὰ χερσίν is ‘in her hands’. The ano teleia announces her speech.

sentences.t:
ἆνερ ἀπ’ αἰῶνος νέος ὤλεο, κὰδ δέ με χήρην
λείπεις ἐν μεγάροισι·
sentences.l:
“Husband, young from life you have perished, and me, a widow,
you leave behind in the halls;
sentences.i: “Husband, you have perished from life while still young, and you leave me a widow in the halls;
sentences.n: Andromache’s lament begins. ἆνερ is ὦ ἄνερ, ‘O husband’. ὤλεο is the aorist of the middle ὄλλυμαι ‘perish’; ἀπ’ αἰῶνος is ‘away from life’ and νέος ‘young’. κὰδ … λείπεις is καταλείπεις ‘leave behind’ with the preverb apart (tmesis), its τ made δ before δέ. με χήρην is ‘me a widow’.

sentences.t:
πάϊς δ’ ἔτι νήπιος αὔτως
ὃν τέκομεν σύ τ’ ἐγώ τε δυσάμμοροι, οὐδέ μιν οἴω
ἥβην ἵξεσθαι·
sentences.i: and our child is still a mere infant, whom you and I, ill-fated both, brought into the world, and I do not think he will reach his youth;
sentences.n: πάϊς is παῖς ‘child’ (the diaeresis shows two syllables), their small son. αὔτως is ‘just so’, merely, as he is. ὃν τέκομεν ‘whom we bore’ is the aorist of τίκτω, here said of both parents, without the augment. δυσάμμοροι ‘ill-fated’ is nominative plural for the two of them: δυσ- ‘ill’ + ἄμμορος ‘without a share’. οἴω is οἴομαι ‘I think’, and ἵξεσθαι the future infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’; ἥβη is ‘youth’, the strength of young manhood.

sentences.t:
πρὶν γὰρ πόλις ἥδε κατ’ ἄκρης
πέρσεται·
sentences.l:
for before then this city from the top down
will be sacked;
sentences.i: for this city will be sacked from top to bottom before then;
sentences.n: πρὶν γάρ ‘for before (that)’ gives the reason for doubting that he will grow up. κατ’ ἄκρης is ‘from the top down’, that is, utterly. πέρσεται is the future middle of πέρθω ‘sack’, with passive sense: ‘will be sacked’.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ ὄλωλας ἐπίσκοπος, ὅς τέ μιν αὐτὴν
ῥύσκευ, ἔχες δ’ ἀλόχους κεδνὰς καὶ νήπια τέκνα,
αἳ δή τοι τάχα νηυσὶν ὀχήσονται γλαφυρῇσι,
καὶ μὲν ἐγὼ μετὰ τῇσι·
sentences.l:
for truly you have perished, a guardian, who it itself
used to protect, and you kept trusty wives and infant children,
who indeed soon in hollow ships will be carried,
and moreover I among them;
sentences.i: for you have perished who were its guardian, you who used to protect it and kept trusty wives and little children, who will soon be carried in hollow ships, and I among them;
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ ‘for truly’ begins the reason: Hector was the city’s guardian. An ἐπίσκοπος is one who watches over. ὅς τέ is the relative with the epic τε, and μιν αὐτήν ‘it itself’ is the city. ῥύσκευ is the iterative imperfect of ῥύομαι ‘protect’, ‘you used to protect’. ἔχες ‘you kept’ takes ἀλόχους κεδνάς ‘trusty wives’ and νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’; the relative αἳ is feminine, so it points to the wives, and the children go with them in the thought. τοι is ‘you see’, τάχα ‘soon’. ὀχήσονται is the future of ὀχέω ‘carry’, passive in sense: ‘will be carried’. καὶ μὲν ἐγώ is ‘and moreover I’, with μετὰ τῇσι ‘among them’.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ αὖ τέκος ἢ ἐμοὶ αὐτῇ
ἕψεαι, ἔνθά κεν ἔργα ἀεικέα ἐργάζοιο
ἀθλεύων πρὸ ἄνακτος ἀμειλίχου,
sentences.l:
and you, in turn, child, either with me myself
will follow, where unseemly works you would work,
labouring before a lord, ungentle,
sentences.i: and you in turn, child, will either follow me myself to where you would do unseemly work, labouring before an unrelenting lord,
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ αὖ τέκος: she turns from Hector to her son, ‘and you, in turn, child’. ἕψεαι is the future of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ in the uncontracted epic form (= ἕψῃ). It begins an ‘either … or’: the ἤ of the next unit (ἤ τις Ἀχαιῶν) gives the second choice. ἔνθά κεν … ἐργάζοιο is ‘where you would work’, an optative with κεν; ἔργα ἀεικέα ‘unseemly works’. ἀθλεύων is ‘toiling’, as a servant; πρὸ ἄνακτος ἀμειλίχου is ‘before an ungentle lord’, working under the eye of a master who does not relent.

sentences.t:
ἤ τις Ἀχαιῶν
ῥίψει χειρὸς ἑλὼν ἀπὸ πύργου λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον
χωόμενος,
sentences.l:
or some one of the Achaeans
will throw you, seizing by the hand, from a tower, a grievous destruction,
incensed,
sentences.i: or some Achaean, incensed, will seize you by the hand and throw you from a tower to grievous destruction,
sentences.n: ἤ τις Ἀχαιῶν is the second alternative after the ἢ of the last unit. ῥίψει is the future of ῥίπτω ‘throw’; χειρὸς ἑλών ‘taking by the hand’ has the genitive of the part grasped. ἀπὸ πύργου is ‘from a tower’, and λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον ‘a grievous destruction’ stands in apposition as the outcome of the throw. The object ‘you’ is not stated. χωόμενος ‘incensed’ gives the man’s motive, which the next unit explains.

sentences.t:
ᾧ δή που ἀδελφεὸν ἔκτανεν Ἕκτωρ
ἢ πατέρ’ ἠὲ καὶ υἱόν, ἐπεὶ μάλα πολλοὶ Ἀχαιῶν
Ἕκτορος ἐν παλάμῃσιν ὀδὰξ ἕλον ἄσπετον οὖδας.
sentences.l:
whose, I suppose, brother Hector killed
or father or even son, since very many of the Achaeans
at Hector’s hands with their teeth bit the boundless ground.
sentences.i: someone whose brother, I suppose, Hector killed, or father, or even son; for very many of the Achaeans have bitten the boundless earth with their teeth at Hector’s hands.
sentences.n: ᾧ is a relative in the dative of interest, ‘to whom … a brother’, that is, ‘whose brother’; δή που is ‘I suppose’. ἢ … ἠέ ‘or … or’. ἔκτανεν is the aorist of κτείνω ‘kill’. ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας ‘took the ground with their teeth’ is a fixed phrase for falling in battle, ‘bit the earth’; ἄσπετον ‘boundless’ goes with οὖδας ‘ground’. ἐν παλάμῃσιν is ‘in the hands’, that is, at Hector’s hands.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ μείλιχος ἔσκε πατὴρ τεὸς ἐν δαῒ λυγρῇ·
sentences.l: for not gentle was your father in grievous battle;
sentences.i: for your father was not gentle in grievous battle;
sentences.n: μείλιχος ‘gentle’ goes with ἔσκε, an iterative form of εἰμί ‘used to be’, here simply ‘was’. τεός is the epic σός ‘your’. ἐν δαῒ λυγρῇ is ‘in grievous battle’ (δαΐ, with a diaeresis, is the dative of δαΐς ‘battle’). The line says why an Achaean would want revenge on Hector’s son.

sentences.t:
τὼ καί μιν λαοὶ μὲν ὀδύρονται κατὰ ἄστυ,
ἀρητὸν δὲ τοκεῦσι γόον καὶ πένθος ἔθηκας
Ἕκτορ·
sentences.i: that is why the people lament him through the town, and you have brought your parents a cursed lament and grief, Hector;
sentences.n: τὼ is τῷ ‘therefore’. καί μιν ‘him too’: the people lament him as she does; ὀδύρονται ‘lament’; κατὰ ἄστυ ‘through the town’. She then addresses Hector himself (Ἕκτορ, at the end). The meaning of ἀρητόν is not certain: it is from ἀρά ‘prayer, curse’, and ‘accursed’ is the usual guess. γόον καὶ πένθος ἔθηκας is ‘you made lament and grief’, with τοκεῦσι ‘for parents’ in the dative of interest.

sentences.t: ἐμοὶ δὲ μάλιστα λελείψεται ἄλγεα λυγρά.
sentences.l: but to me most of all will be left grievous pains.
sentences.i: but to me, above all, grievous pains will be left.
sentences.n: ἐμοὶ δὲ μάλιστα is ‘but to me most of all’. λελείψεται is the future perfect passive of λείπω, ‘will remain left’, a state that will last. ἄλγεα are ‘pains’ and λυγρά ‘grievous’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μοι θνῄσκων λεχέων ἐκ χεῖρας ὄρεξας,
οὐδέ τί μοι εἶπες πυκινὸν ἔπος, οὗ τέ κεν αἰεὶ
μεμνῄμην νύκτάς τε καὶ ἤματα δάκρυ χέουσα.
sentences.i: for as you died you did not stretch out your hands to me from a bed, and you spoke no solid word to me that I might remember always, night and day, shedding tears.”
sentences.n: This gives the reason for ‘most of all’: Hector left her no parting gesture or word. θνῄσκων is ‘dying’ (‘as you were dying’); λεχέων ἐκ is ‘from the bed’ (the poetic plural again), the deathbed of a man who dies at home, which Hector, killed in battle, did not have. ὄρεξας is the aorist of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’. πυκινὸν ἔπος is a ‘close-packed’ word, one with weight, in the house rendering ‘solid word’. οὗ is the genitive relative after μεμνῄμην, the perfect optative of μιμνῄσκομαι, ‘I would remember’, with κεν. νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα ‘nights and days’ is an accusative of duration, and δάκρυ χέουσα ‘a tear shedding’ is the feminine of the stock phrase. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσ’, ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γυναῖκες.
sentences.l: So she spoke weeping, and groaned in answer the women.
sentences.i: So she spoke, weeping, and the women groaned in answer.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο ‘so she spoke’ closes a speech, with κλαίουσ’ (κλαίουσα) ‘weeping’. ἐπὶ δὲ στενάχοντο γυναῖκες is ‘and in answer the women groaned’: ἐπί is an adverb, ‘in answer’, as in 722, and the women answer each lament with groans.

sentences.t: τῇσιν δ’ αὖθ’ Ἑκάβη ἁδινοῦ ἐξῆρχε γόοιο·
sentences.l: And for them in turn Hecuba led off the thronging lament:
sentences.i: And among them in turn Hecuba led off the thronging lament:
sentences.n: Hecuba, Hector’s mother, is the second to lead. τῇσιν ‘for them’ is the women; αὖθ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’. ἁδινοῦ γόοιο is ‘the thronging lament’, and ἐξῆρχε ‘led off’ takes the genitive γόοιο, as Andromache’s ἦρχε did at 723.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἐμῷ θυμῷ πάντων πολὺ φίλτατε παίδων,
ἦ μέν μοι ζωός περ ἐὼν φίλος ἦσθα θεοῖσιν·
sentences.l:
“Hector, to my heart of all the children by far dearest,
truly to me, even living, dear you were to the gods;
sentences.i: “Hector, by far the dearest to my heart of all my children, truly, even while you lived you were dear to the gods;
sentences.n: Hecuba’s speech begins. ἐμῷ θυμῷ ‘to my heart’ is a dative of feeling; πάντων … παίδων ‘of all my children’ is partitive, and πολύ ‘by far’ strengthens the superlative vocative φίλτατε. ἦ μέν ‘truly’; μοι ‘to me’ is a dative of feeling too, as if to say ‘as I see it’. ζωός περ ἐών is ‘even while living’, and θεοῖσιν (epic dative plural) depends on φίλος ‘dear to’.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἄρα σεῦ κήδοντο καὶ ἐν θανάτοιό περ αἴσῃ.
sentences.l: and they of you cared even in the lot of death.
sentences.i: and they cared for you still, even in the lot of death.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they, then’, the gods. σεῦ is the epic genitive of σύ, governed by κήδοντο, the imperfect of κήδομαι ‘care for’. ἐν θανάτοιό περ αἴσῃ is ‘even in the lot of death’: αἶσα ‘portion, lot’, θανάτοιο the epic genitive. The gods, she says, did not stop caring when he died.

sentences.t:
ἄλλους μὲν γὰρ παῖδας ἐμοὺς πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεὺς
πέρνασχ’ ὅν τιν’ ἕλεσκε πέρην ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο,
ἐς Σάμον ἔς τ’ Ἴμβρον καὶ Λῆμνον ἀμιχθαλόεσσαν·
sentences.i: Other children of mine Achilles, swift of foot, used to sell across the sea that yields no harvest, whomever he caught, to Samos and to Imbros and to misty Lemnos;
sentences.n: γάρ introduces the proof that the gods care for Hector: Achilles sold her other children. πέρνασχ’ is πέρνασκε, the iterative imperfect of πέρνημι ‘sell’ (‘used to sell’), and ἕλεσκε the iterative of αἱρέω ‘take’, so ὅν τιν’ ἕλεσκε is ‘whomever he caught’. πέρην ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο is ‘across the sea’; ἀτρυγέτοιο, the sea’s epithet, is rendered ‘that yields no harvest’, but its meaning is not known. Σάμον, Ἴμβρον and Λῆμνον are islands of the northern Aegean (this Samos is the Thracian one, later called Samothrace). ἀμιχθαλόεσσαν, the epithet of Lemnos, is of unknown meaning; ‘misty’ is only a guess.

sentences.t:
σεῦ δ’ ἐπεὶ ἐξέλετο ψυχὴν ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ,
πολλὰ ῥυστάζεσκεν ἑοῦ περὶ σῆμ’ ἑτάροιο
Πατρόκλου, τὸν ἔπεφνες·
sentences.i: but when he had taken your soul out with long-pointed bronze, he dragged you about, again and again, round the tomb of his own companion Patroclus, whom you slew;
sentences.n: σεῦ δ’ ἐπεί ‘but you, when’: σεῦ is the genitive of σύ, with ψυχήν ‘soul’. ἐξέλετο is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’; ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ ‘long-pointed bronze’. ῥυστάζεσκεν is an iterative of ῥυστάζω ‘drag’, and πολλά ‘many times’; the object, Hector, is understood from σεῦ. ἑοῦ … ἑτάροιο is ‘of his own companion’ (ἑοῦ is the possessive ‘his own’), and σῆμα is the tomb. ἔπεφνες is the aorist of φένω ‘slay’, without the augment.

sentences.t: ἀνέστησεν δέ μιν οὐδ’ ὧς.
sentences.l: but did not raise him up, not even so.
sentences.i: yet not even so did he raise him up.
sentences.n: ἀνέστησεν is the aorist of ἀνίστημι used transitively, ‘raised up’. μιν ‘him’ is Patroclus, not Hector: even the dragging of Hector’s body did not bring Patroclus back. οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘not even so’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ μοι ἑρσήεις καὶ πρόσφατος ἐν μεγάροισι
κεῖσαι, τῷ ἴκελος ὅν τ’ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
οἷς ἀγανοῖσι βέλεσσιν ἐποιχόμενος κατέπεφνεν.
sentences.l:
but now to me dewy and fresh, in the halls
you lie, like to him whom silver-bowed Apollo
with his gentle shafts, assailing, slew.”
sentences.i: But now you lie in my halls, dewy and fresh, like one whom silver-bowed Apollo came upon with his gentle arrows and killed.”
sentences.n: νῦν δέ μοι is ‘but now, for me’. ἑρσήεις ‘dewy’ and πρόσφατος ‘fresh’ (of a body newly dead): Hector lies unspoiled, as if dew had just fallen on him. κεῖσαι is the second person singular of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. τῷ ἴκελος ὅν τε is ‘like him whom’, a comparison with a man killed by Apollo. ἀργυρότοξος ‘silver-bowed’ is a stock epithet. ἀγανοῖσι βέλεσσιν is ‘with gentle arrows’: Apollo’s arrows are gentle because they bring a sudden, painless death. ἐποιχόμενος is ‘coming upon’, and κατέπεφνεν the aorist ‘slew’. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσα, γόον δ’ ἀλίαστον ὄρινε.
sentences.l: So she spoke weeping, and a lament relentless she stirred up.
sentences.i: So she spoke, weeping, and stirred up a relentless lament.
sentences.n: ὄρινε is the unaugmented past of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’. ἀλίαστον ‘relentless’ is of uncertain origin, perhaps ἀ- ‘not’ + λιάζομαι ‘bend aside’, a lament that does not give way.

sentences.t: τῇσι δ’ ἔπειθ’ Ἑλένη τριτάτη ἐξῆρχε γόοιο·
sentences.l: And for them thereupon Helen, third, led off the lament:
sentences.i: Then Helen, third, led off the lament among them:
sentences.n: Helen is the third to lead. τῇσι ‘for them’ is the women; ἔπειθ’ is ἔπειτα ‘thereupon’; τριτάτη ‘third’ is in order of leading. ἐξῆρχε γόοιο ‘led off the lament’, as for Hecuba.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἐμῷ θυμῷ δαέρων πολὺ φίλτατε πάντων,
ἦ μέν μοι πόσις ἐστὶν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδής,
ὅς μ’ ἄγαγε Τροίηνδ’·
sentences.i: “Hector, by far the dearest to my heart of all my husband’s brothers, truly my husband is Alexander, godlike in form, who brought me to Troy;
sentences.n: Helen’s speech begins. Hector is δαέρων … φίλτατε πάντων, ‘dearest of all my husband’s brothers’: δαήρ is ‘husband’s brother’, here in the genitive plural δαέρων. Her husband is Alexander, the other name of Paris; θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ is his stock epithet, kept. ἄγαγε is the aorist of ἄγω ‘lead’ without the augment, and Τροίηνδ’ is Τροίηνδε ‘to Troy’ with the suffix -δε of direction.

sentences.t: ὡς πρὶν ὤφελλον ὀλέσθαι.
sentences.l: would that before then I had perished.
sentences.i: if only I had perished before then.
sentences.n: ὡς … ὤφελλον ὀλέσθαι is ‘would that I had perished’: ὡς introduces the wish, ὤφελλον is the imperfect of ὀφέλλω in the sense ‘ought’, ‘would that’, and ὀλέσθαι the aorist infinitive of ὄλλυμαι. πρίν is ‘before (that)’, before Alexander brought her.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ νῦν μοι τόδε εἰκοστὸν ἔτος ἐστὶν
ἐξ οὗ κεῖθεν ἔβην καὶ ἐμῆς ἀπελήλυθα πάτρης·
sentences.l:
For already now to me this is the twentieth year
since I went from there and from my fatherland have gone away;
sentences.i: For it is already the twentieth year for me now since I left that place and went away from my fatherland;
sentences.n: ἤδη … νῦν ‘already now’. εἰκοστὸν ἔτος is ‘the twentieth year’, counted ἐξ οὗ ‘from when’ she left. κεῖθεν is ‘from there’, ἔβην the aorist of βαίνω ‘go’, and ἀπελήλυθα the perfect of ἀπέρχομαι, ‘I have gone away’; ἐμῆς … πάτρης ‘from my fatherland’ is the genitive after the ἀπο- of the verb.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πω σεῦ ἄκουσα κακὸν ἔπος οὐδ’ ἀσύφηλον·
sentences.l: but never yet have I heard from you an evil word nor a disgraceful one;
sentences.i: but I have never yet heard an evil or disgraceful word from you;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὔ πω is ‘but never yet’. σεῦ ἄκουσα is ‘I heard from you’: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard. ἀσύφηλον is a word of unknown meaning; ‘disgraceful’ is a guess from the context, set against κακὸν ἔπος ‘evil word’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴ τίς με καὶ ἄλλος ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἐνίπτοι
δαέρων ἢ γαλόων ἢ εἰνατέρων εὐπέπλων,
ἢ ἑκυρή, ἑκυρὸς δὲ πατὴρ ὣς ἤπιος αἰεί,
sentences.l:
but if any other too in the halls rebuked me,
of my husband’s brothers, or my husband’s sisters, or my husband’s brothers’ wives, fair-robed,
or mother-in-law — but father-in-law, a father, so kind always —
sentences.i: But if anyone else in the halls rebuked me, one of my husband’s brothers, or my husband’s sisters, or my husband’s brothers’ fair-robed wives, or my mother-in-law (my father-in-law is always as kind as a father) —
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ εἴ τίς με καὶ ἄλλος … ἐνίπτοι is ‘but if anyone else too rebuked me’, an optative for a case that may arise. The three genitives say who: δαέρων ‘of (my husband’s) brothers’, γαλόων ‘of (my husband’s) sisters’, εἰνατέρων εὐπέπλων ‘of (my husband’s) brothers’ wives, fair-robed’ (εὔπεπλος is a stock epithet of women). ἢ ἑκυρή is ‘or my mother-in-law’, that is, Hecuba, who has just spoken. The parenthesis ἑκυρὸς δὲ πατὴρ ὣς ἤπιος αἰεί is about Priam, ‘but my father-in-law, a father, so kind always’; the printed ὣς is ‘so’, and the sense is that he is as kind as a father should be. The line 769 is metrically irregular as transmitted: δαέρων, whose first syllable is short at 762, opens the line and can scan only if it is read with its first two vowels run together or with δα- long and its final -ρων shortened before ἢ, and the fifth foot comes out as a spondee.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ τὸν ἐπέεσσι παραιφάμενος κατέρυκες
σῇ τ’ ἀγανοφροσύνῃ καὶ σοῖς ἀγανοῖς ἐπέεσσι.
sentences.l:
but you him with words talking-round restrained,
with your gentleness of mind and with your gentle words.
sentences.i: you would coax him round with words and hold him back, with your gentleness of mind and your gentle words.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ σὺ τόν is ‘yet you … him’, the one who rebuked her. κατέρυκες is the imperfect of κατερύκω ‘hold back’ (‘you used to hold him back’), and παραιφάμενος the participle of παράφημι ‘talk round, coax’. σῇ τ’ ἀγανοφροσύνῃ is ‘with your gentleness of mind’ (ἀγανός ‘gentle’ + φρήν ‘mind’), and σοῖς ἀγανοῖς ἐπέεσσι ‘with your gentle words’, the epic dative plural of ἔπος.

sentences.t: τὼ σέ θ’ ἅμα κλαίω καὶ ἔμ’ ἄμμορον ἀχνυμένη κῆρ·
sentences.l: therefore you at the same time I weep and me, ill-fated, grieving in heart;
sentences.i: so I weep for you and for myself together, ill-fated, grieving in heart;
sentences.n: τὼ ‘therefore’. σέ θ’ ἅμα … καὶ ἔμ’ is ‘you and me together’ (θ’ is τε), both objects of κλαίω ‘I weep’. ἄμμορον ‘ill-fated’ (ἄ- + μόρος ‘portion’) agrees with ἔμ’, and ἀχνυμένη κῆρ is ‘grieving in heart’, κῆρ being an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τίς μοι ἔτ’ ἄλλος ἐνὶ Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ
ἤπιος οὐδὲ φίλος, πάντες δέ με πεφρίκασιν.
sentences.l:
for not any other to me still in broad Troy
is kind nor friendly, and all bristle at me.”
sentences.i: for there is no one else left in broad Troy who is kind or friendly to me, and all bristle with fear at me.”
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ τις … ἔτ’ ἄλλος is ‘for no one else any longer’. ἐνὶ Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ is ‘in broad Troy’ (εὐρείῃ is the feminine dative); ἤπιος οὐδὲ φίλος is ‘kind or friendly’. πεφρίκασιν is the perfect of φρίσσω ‘bristle’ with present sense: they bristle at her with fear, shrinking from her. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατο κλαίουσ’, ἐπὶ δ’ ἔστενε δῆμος ἀπείρων.
sentences.l: So she spoke weeping, and in answer groaned the people, boundless.
sentences.i: So she spoke, weeping, and the boundless people groaned in answer.
sentences.n: ἔστενε is the imperfect of στένω ‘groan’, and ἐπί again the adverb ‘in answer’. δῆμος is the people here, and ἀπείρων ‘boundless’ makes them a crowd without number.

sentences.t: λαοῖσιν δ’ ὃ γέρων Πρίαμος μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and among the people the old man Priam a speech spoke:
sentences.i: Then the old man Priam spoke among the people:
sentences.n: λαοῖσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘to / among the people’. ὃ γέρων Πρίαμος is ‘he, the old man Priam’, ὃ being the pronoun that later became the article. μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπεν is ‘spoke a speech among them’, a stock line to open a speech; ἔειπεν is the Homeric aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t:
ἄξετε νῦν Τρῶες ξύλα ἄστυ δέ, μὴ δέ τι θυμῷ
δείσητ’ Ἀργείων πυκινὸν λόχον·
sentences.l:
“Bring now, Trojans, wood to the town, and do not at all in heart
fear the solid ambush of the Argives;
sentences.i: “Bring wood to the town now, Trojans, and do not fear in your hearts a solid ambush of the Argives;
sentences.n: Priam’s speech begins. ἄξετε is a command, a future form of ἄγω ‘lead, bring’ used as an imperative. ξύλα are the logs of wood for the pyre, and ἄστυ δέ is ἄστυδε ‘to the town’, the suffix -δε giving direction. μὴ δέ τι … δείσητ’ is ‘and do not at all fear’: the aorist subjunctive after μή makes a prohibition. θυμῷ is ‘in your heart’, and πυκινὸν λόχον ‘a solid ambush’.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
πέμπων μ’ ὧδ’ ἐπέτελλε μελαινάων ἀπὸ νηῶν
μὴ πρὶν πημανέειν πρὶν δωδεκάτη μόλῃ ἠώς.
sentences.i: for when Achilles sent me from the black ships he charged them not to do harm before the twelfth dawn has come.”
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ ‘for truly’ gives the reason for not fearing. πέμπων μ’ ὧδ’ is ‘sending me thus’, and ἐπέτελλε the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘give charge’, followed by μὴ … πημανέειν ‘not to do harm’, with the Achaeans as the unstated subject; πημανέειν is the epic uncontracted future infinitive of πημαίνω. πρὶν … πρὶν: the first is ‘before’ as an adverb, the second the conjunction ‘before (the time when)’, with the aorist subjunctive μόλῃ (from βλώσκω ‘come’) and no κε. δωδεκάτη ἠώς is ‘the twelfth dawn’, and μελαινάων ἀπὸ νηῶν ‘from the black ships’ (epic genitive plural). His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ὑπ’ ἀμάξῃσιν βόας ἡμιόνους τε
ζεύγνυσαν, αἶψα δ’ ἔπειτα πρὸ ἄστεος ἠγερέθοντο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they under the wagons oxen and mules
yoked, and quickly then before the town assembled.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they yoked oxen and mules to the wagons, and quickly gathered before the town.
sentences.n: ὑπ’ ἀμάξῃσιν is ‘under the wagons’, that is, to their yokes; βόας ἡμιόνους τε are ‘oxen and mules’. ζεύγνυσαν is the imperfect of ζεύγνυμι ‘yoke’, and ἠγερέθοντο the imperfect of ἠγερέθομαι ‘gather’, both plural for the crowd. πρὸ ἄστεος is ‘before the town’, outside it. ἔφαθ’ as at 718.

sentences.t: ἐννῆμαρ μὲν τοί γε ἀγίνεον ἄσπετον ὕλην·
sentences.l: Nine days they, for their part, were bringing boundless forest;
sentences.i: For nine days they were bringing in boundless forest;
sentences.n: ἐννῆμαρ is ‘for nine days’. ἀγίνεον is the imperfect of ἀγινέω ‘bring’ in its uncontracted form. ἄσπετον ‘boundless’ goes with ὕλην, ‘forest’ in the sense of timber cut for the pyre. τοί γε is ‘they, for their part’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ δεκάτη ἐφάνη φαεσίμβροτος ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ ἐξέφερον θρασὺν Ἕκτορα δάκρυ χέοντες,
ἐν δὲ πυρῇ ὑπάτῃ νεκρὸν θέσαν, ἐν δ’ ἔβαλον πῦρ.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the tenth appeared, the mortal-lighting dawn,
then they carried out bold Hector, a tear shedding,
and on the topmost pyre the corpse they placed, and in they threw fire.
sentences.i: But when the tenth dawn appeared, the dawn that gives light to mortals, then they carried bold Hector out, shedding tears, and set the corpse on the topmost pyre and threw fire in.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή is ‘but when at last’. δεκάτη ‘tenth’ goes with ἠώς ‘dawn’, and φαεσίμβροτος ‘giving light to mortals’ is its stock epithet; ἐφάνη is the aorist passive of φαίνω ‘appear’. ἐξέφερον is ‘were carrying out’, and θρασὺν Ἕκτορα ‘bold Hector’. ἐν δὲ πυρῇ ὑπάτῃ … θέσαν is ‘and on the topmost pyre they placed’, ὑπάτῃ being ‘highest’; ἐν … ἔβαλον is tmesis for ἐνέβαλον, ‘threw in’, so they set the pyre alight.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
τῆμος ἄρ’ ἀμφὶ πυρὴν κλυτοῦ Ἕκτορος ἔγρετο λαός.
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then around the pyre of famous Hector awoke the people.
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, then the people woke around the pyre of famous Hector.
sentences.n: ἦμος … τῆμος is ‘when … then’. ἠριγένεια ‘early-born’ and ῥοδοδάκτυλος ‘rose-fingered’ are Dawn’s stock epithets, kept each time; the first line is the familiar dawn-formula. ἀμφὶ πυρήν is ‘around the pyre’, and κλυτοῦ Ἕκτορος ‘famous Hector’. ἔγρετο is the aorist middle of ἐγείρω, ‘woke’: the people wake where they are, around the pyre.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἤγερθεν ὁμηγερέες τ’ ἐγένοντο
πρῶτον μὲν κατὰ πυρκαϊὴν σβέσαν αἴθοπι οἴνῳ
πᾶσαν, ὁπόσσον ἐπέσχε πυρὸς μένος·
sentences.i: When they had gathered and were all assembled, first they quenched the pyre with wine that has the look of fire, all of it, as far as the might of the fire had reached;
sentences.n: ἤγερθεν is the aorist passive of ἀγείρω ‘gather’; ὁμηγερέες is ‘gathered together’, and ἐγένοντο ‘had become’. πρῶτον μέν ‘first’ is answered by αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα in the next unit. κατὰ … σβέσαν is tmesis for κατέσβεσαν ‘quenched’, with αἴθοπι οἴνῳ ‘fire-faced wine’ (αἴθοψ is αἴθω ‘burn’ + ὤψ ‘face, look’). πᾶσαν ‘all of it’ goes with πυρκαϊήν ‘the pyre’, and ὁπόσσον ἐπέσχε πυρὸς μένος is ‘as far as the might of the fire had reached’, ἐπέσχε being the aorist of ἐπέχω ‘extend over’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
ὀστέα λευκὰ λέγοντο κασίγνητοί θ’ ἕταροί τε
μυρόμενοι, θαλερὸν δὲ κατείβετο δάκρυ παρειῶν.
sentences.l:
but then
the white bones were gathering brothers and companions,
mourning, and an abundant tear flowed down from their cheeks.
sentences.i: Then his brothers and companions gathered up the white bones, mourning, while an abundant tear ran down from their cheeks.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘but then’ answers πρῶτον μέν in the previous unit. ὀστέα λευκά are ‘the white bones’. λέγοντο is the imperfect middle of λέγω in its old sense ‘gather up’, and κασίγνητοι ‘brothers’ and ἕταροι ‘companions’ are its subject (θ’ … τε is ‘both … and’). μυρόμενοι ‘mourning’. θαλερὸν δάκρυ ‘an abundant tear’; κατείβετο is the imperfect middle of κατείβω ‘let flow down’, here intransitive, ‘ran down’; παρειῶν ‘from the cheeks’ is a genitive.

sentences.t:
καὶ τά γε χρυσείην ἐς λάρνακα θῆκαν ἑλόντες
πορφυρέοις πέπλοισι καλύψαντες μαλακοῖσιν.
sentences.l:
and these into a golden chest they put, having taken them,
with purple robes covering them, soft ones.
sentences.i: These they took up and put in a golden chest, covering them over with soft purple robes.
sentences.n: τά γε ‘those’ are the bones. χρυσείην ἐς λάρνακα is ‘into a golden chest’; a λάρναξ is a chest or box, here the casket for the bones. θῆκαν = ἔθηκαν, and ἑλόντες is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, ‘having taken (them up)’. πορφυρέοις πέπλοισι … μαλακοῖσιν is ‘with soft purple robes’; the adjective μαλακοῖσιν is set after its noun, and καλύψαντες is ‘covering’.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ ἐς κοίλην κάπετον θέσαν, αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε
πυκνοῖσιν λάεσσι κατεστόρεσαν μεγάλοισι·
sentences.l:
and at once into a hollow ditch they placed it, and above
with solid stones they spread it over, great ones;
sentences.i: At once they placed it in a hollow grave, and spread great, solid stones over it;
sentences.n: αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and at once’. κοίλην κάπετον is ‘a hollow ditch’: a κάπετος is a dug trench, here the grave-pit, so the English says ‘grave’. The chest is the unstated object of θέσαν ‘placed’. αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε is ‘and above’. κατεστόρεσαν is the aorist of καταστορέννυμι ‘spread over’, with the stones in the dative: πυκνοῖσιν λάεσσι … μεγάλοισι is ‘with solid stones, great ones’ (πυκνός is the short form of πυκινός, and λάεσσι the epic dative of λᾶας ‘stone’).

sentences.t:
ῥίμφα δὲ σῆμ’ ἔχεαν, περὶ δὲ σκοποὶ ἥατο πάντῃ,
μὴ πρὶν ἐφορμηθεῖεν ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
and nimbly a tomb they heaped, and around lookouts sat on every side,
lest sooner they should rush upon them, the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: They heaped up the tomb nimbly, with lookouts sitting all around, lest the well-greaved Achaeans should rush upon them before the time.
sentences.n: ῥίμφα is ‘nimbly’. σῆμα ἔχεαν is ‘heaped a tomb’: ἔχεαν is the aorist of χέω ‘pour, heap’ (the earth is not named), and the σῆμα is the mound. περὶ δὲ σκοποὶ ἥατο πάντῃ is ‘and around lookouts sat on every side’; ἥατο is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’, with the Ionic ending -ατο. μὴ πρὶν ἐφορμηθεῖεν is ‘lest sooner they rush upon (them)’: an aorist passive optative of ἐφορμάομαι ‘rush upon’, after a past tense, giving the lookouts’ purpose. ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί ‘the well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock phrase.

sentences.t: χεύαντες δὲ τὸ σῆμα πάλιν κίον·
sentences.l: and having heaped the tomb, back they went;
sentences.i: When they had heaped up the tomb, they went back;
sentences.n: χεύαντες is the aorist participle of χέω ‘heap’, and πάλιν ‘back’. κίον is the third plural of κίω ‘go’, without the augment: ‘they went’. The ano teleia closes the burial and turns to the feast.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
εὖ συναγειρόμενοι δαίνυντ’ ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα
δώμασιν ἐν Πριάμοιο διοτρεφέος βασιλῆος.
sentences.l:
and then
well assembling together, they feasted a glorious feast
in the halls of Priam, Zeus-nurtured king.
sentences.i: and then, gathering well together, they feasted on a glorious feast in the halls of Priam, the Zeus-nurtured king.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘and then’. εὖ συναγειρόμενοι is ‘gathering well together’, εὖ being ‘well’, in good order. δαίνυντ’ is δαίνυντο ‘feasted’, with ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα ‘a glorious feast’ as its object, ‘feasted a feast’. δώμασιν ἐν Πριάμοιο διοτρεφέος βασιλῆος is ‘in the halls of Priam, the Zeus-nurtured king’: δώματα is the poetic plural ‘halls’, διοτρεφέος ‘Zeus-nurtured’ (Διός + τρέφω) and βασιλῆος the epic genitive.

sentences.t: ὣς οἵ γ’ ἀμφίεπον τάφον Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο.
sentences.l: So they busied themselves about the burial of Hector, horse-taming.
sentences.i: So they busied themselves with the funeral of Hector, tamer of horses.
sentences.n: ὣς οἵ γ’ is ‘so they’. ἀμφίεπον is the imperfect of ἀμφιέπω ‘busy oneself about’. τάφον here is ‘burial’, a different word from τάφος ‘amazement’. Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο is ‘of Hector, tamer of horses’, with the stock epithet ἱππόδαμος ‘horse-taming’ in the epic genitive. This is the last line of the Iliad.
